svg.title: Bench breadboard layout — Teensy board, drive-sensor board, steering-sensor board
svg.desc: Three half-size breadboards wired for bench bring-up. Board A carries the Teensy 4.1 straddling the centre channel, with its 3V3 pin feeding the lower plus rail and rail-bridge jumpers carrying that supply to the upper rails; 10k pull-ups and 1nF capacitors sit on the two quadrature input columns and 4.7k pull-ups on the I2C columns. Board B carries the two TO-92 Hall latches, board C the AS5600 breakout, so drive and steering can be worked in parallel and each maps onto its own harness later. Wire crossings are drawn with gaps where there is no connection.
svg.text: Bench layout — three boards, and every supply traced back to the Teensy's own 3V3 pin
A pale column band marks one electrical node — anything landing in it is connected. A gap in a wire means it passes over, not into.
Pin numbers are provisional — 04-firmware has not pinned them, which is the whole reason this stage is on a breadboard.

Why drive and steering are
on separate boards
They become two harnesses at two
ends of the vehicle — a rear hub and
a front kingpin. Splitting them here
means each bench board transfers
to its own perfboard section.
It also lets two people work in
parallel — one waving a magnet,
one rotating one.
Three boards per station — and nothing more to order
9 breadboards = 3 stations × 3. Exactly what was bought.
AS5600 ×5 covers it, because the bench unit is the one you then fit
to that vehicle — which is better anyway, since AGC is tuned per part.
3 fitted + 1 benched-then-fitted + spares. No separate bench stock needed.

text.tspan: The drive board needs no AS5600 and the steering board needs no latches.

svg.text: Splitting them costs one breadboard and buys a harness-shaped bench.
Jumper sets ×3 — one per station — is also right.
After the VUSB–VIN cut: USB is data only
Yes. The laptop still programs it and still carries micro-ROS. It just
cannot power it. 5 V comes from a UBEC into VIN, on the bench and
on the vehicle alike.
The cut exists so the laptop's 5 V and the UBEC's 5 V never meet
and push current into each other through the Teensy.
A Teensy that seems dead on USB after the cut is working correctly.
Tape a note on the lid of the parts box. Somebody will meet this at 11 pm.
Prove it in this order — each step fails for a different reason
1 · Power only. 5 V at VIN. Meter the + rail on board C — the far end of the chain. 3.3 V there proves the 3V3 pin,
both rail bridges and both board-to-board feeds in one reading. Not there → a wire, not a sensor.
2 · Latches, on a meter, before any code. Probe each OUT against GND and pass a magnet by. It must snap between
0 V and 3.3 V and stay there when the magnet leaves — that is what makes it a latch. Falls back on its own →
it is a switch, and the whole quadrature scheme is wrong. Flip the magnet to reset it.
3 · I²C scan. 0x36 must appear, and nothing else — one device per bus is the design.
4 · AGC. Read 0x1A at the working gap, tune to mid-scale, and write the gap down — it is the number the other
two vehicles are built to.
5 · Counts last. Bring up the decoder and move a magnet past both latches in sequence. Up one way and down the
other is the first proof the (n + ½) spacing is right — cheap here, expensive on a wheel.
Steps 1–3 need no firmware beyond a scan sketch. If something is wrong, it is wrong before code can be blamed.
Before a single wire goes in
The TO-92 pin order is not guessable. Legs are drawn 1-2-3 as VCC · GND · OUT, which is the common arrangement —
read the DRV5013 datasheet and confirm it. Reversed VCC/GND destroys the part, which is what the fourteen spares are for,
and it is a far cheaper lesson on a breadboard than on a soldered board.
Keep them in the labelled bag until each one is fitted. TI marks a TO-92 body with an abbreviated code, so loose parts
are unidentifiable and BC looks exactly like AG. Bend the legs out to 2.54 mm — they leave the package closer than that.
Beep the three boards' − rails together before powering up. A missing ground reads as a dead sensor, and on the
vehicle this same joint becomes the star ground at the motor driver.
Nothing on these boards may carry coil current. No relay, no MOSFET, no 12 V — 600 mA through spring clips, and a
floating gate chatters the relays. Signal on breadboard, authority on soldered perfboard.
